newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's shadow legislature to grapple with rights law.
newsitem.headline: HK's shadow legislature to grapple with rights law.

text.p: Hong Kong's controversial provisional legislature will discuss thorny proposals to amend key clauses in the territory's civil and political liberties at a meeting across the border in China on Saturday.
A spokesman for Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Friday the chamber would receive a briefing on responses to a three-week public consultation exercise on the planned curbs.
"At tomorrow's meeting, Michael Suen will brief them on the consultative process and the responses plus what's being considered," Bob Howlett, a spokesman for Tung's office, said.

Suen was seconded from the Hong Kong government to aid Tung as he races to establish his administration ahead of the handover of Hong Kong to China at midnight on June 30, ending more than 150 years of British rule.

The outgoing colonial government, while willing to cooperate with the leader-in-waiting, steadfastly refuses to aid the provisional legislature which it regards as an unconstitutional rival to the existing elected legislature.

Tung's proposed changes, which include introducing police permits for political protests and a ban on foreign funding of local political groups, have sparked an outcry from Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp, local lawyers and human rights activists.

The provisional legislature is forced to hold its meetings in China rather than Hong Kong in order to protect itself from a legal challenge from members of the existing chamber, returned in elections in 1995.
China, angered by the reforms introduced by outgoing British Governor Chris Patten, has ordered the legislature to be disbanded.
The incoming lawmakers will have to draft new electoral laws for polls expected in 1998.
A key member of Tung's government-in-waiting signalled on Wednesday that the planned changes may be watered down.

"There are many proposals that have been put forward to us," Henry Tang, a member of Tung's Executive Council, said. "In the consultation exercise, there are more liberal (proposals) than those in the consultation document."

The provisional legislature is expected to begin work on the new electoral reforms before long, in addition to drafting laws on the right of abode in Hong Kong, the 1997/98 budget and legislation on national and regional flags and emblems.
